lessons.title: Pod: the smallest deployable unit
lessons.summary: A Pod groups one or more tightly coupled containers that share network identity and can share mounted storage.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: A Pod is a scheduling and lifecycle unit, not usually the thing you scale manually for an application. A Deployment manages replicated Pods for most stateless workloads.

sections.heading: What to remember
sections.body: Containers in one Pod share the Pod IP and port space. They can communicate over localhost and may share volumes. Containers in different Pods communicate over the network.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: Do not treat a Pod as a durable server. Pods can be replaced, and a replacement normally has a different identity and IP.

lessons.takeaway: Deploy and scale stateless workloads with a controller such as Deployment; use a Service for a stable network endpoint.

lessons.title: Node: where workloads run
lessons.summary: A Node is a worker machine that provides compute capacity for Pods.

sections.heading: What runs on a node?
sections.body: The kubelet ensures assigned Pods are running, the container runtime runs containers, and networking components provide Pod connectivity.

sections.heading: Scheduling relationship
sections.body: The scheduler selects a suitable node based on resource requests, constraints, taints/tolerations, affinity and other scheduling rules.

sections.heading: Operational signal
sections.body: A Node becoming NotReady can affect many Pods at once. Inspect node conditions and events before assuming each workload has an independent fault.

lessons.takeaway: When many unrelated Pods fail together, inspect shared infrastructure such as the Node before debugging every app separately.

lessons.title: Deployment and ReplicaSet
lessons.summary: A Deployment declares desired state for a replicated stateless workload and manages rollout history.

sections.heading: Control loop
sections.body: The Deployment controller creates or updates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet works to maintain the requested number of matching Pods.

sections.heading: Rollouts
sections.body: A rolling update gradually replaces old Pods with new ones according to rollout strategy settings. Rollout status and history help identify stalled releases.

sections.heading: When not to use it
sections.body: Stateful workloads may need stable identities and ordered storage semantics; evaluate StatefulSet or another controller when those properties matter.

lessons.takeaway: Declare desired state and inspect rollout status; avoid hand-managing individual replicas when a controller is appropriate.

lessons.title: Service: stable network access
lessons.summary: A Service provides a stable virtual endpoint for a changing set of backend Pods.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body: Pod IPs can change as Pods are replaced. A Service selects matching Pods and provides a stable name and virtual IP for clients.

sections.heading: Selector and ports
sections.body: The selector identifies eligible Pods; port and targetPort determine how traffic reaches the workload. A mismatched selector or port can leave a Service without working backends.

sections.heading: Debugging
sections.body: Check the Service selector, EndpointSlices, Pod readiness, and port mapping before changing network policy or application code.

lessons.takeaway: A Service does not create Pods; it routes to eligible backends selected by labels.

lessons.title: Readiness, liveness and startup probes
lessons.summary: Different probes answer different health questions and have different effects on traffic and restarts.

sections.heading: Readiness
sections.body: Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive Service traffic. A not-ready Pod can continue running while it warms up or waits for a dependency.

sections.heading: Liveness
sections.body: Liveness detects a container that should be restarted when it cannot recover on its own. An overly aggressive liveness probe can create restart loops.

sections.heading: Startup
sections.body: Startup probes protect slow-starting applications by delaying liveness and readiness evaluation until startup succeeds.

lessons.takeaway: Readiness gates traffic; liveness triggers restarts; startup protects slow initialization.

references.title: Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes

lessons.title: Resource requests and limits
lessons.summary: Requests inform scheduling; limits constrain resource use according to Kubernetes resource semantics.

sections.heading: Requests
sections.body: The scheduler uses CPU and memory requests when deciding whether a Pod fits on a node. Requests are not a reservation of a fixed CPU core.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: CPU limits can throttle CPU use. Exceeding a memory limit can lead to the container being terminated for out-of-memory conditions.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.body: Correlate Pod events, container termination reason, working-set metrics and node pressure rather than changing limits without evidence.

lessons.takeaway: Requests affect placement; limits constrain use. Tune them using workload measurements and observed failure modes.

references.title: Resource management for Pods and containers

commands.title: List Pods with placement and status
commands.purpose: Inspect Pod readiness, restart counts, IP addresses and node placement at a glance.
commands.environment: kubectl configured for the intended cluster and namespace.
commands.expectedOutput: A table including READY, STATUS, RESTARTS, AGE, IP and NODE columns.
commands.interpretation: Use the namespace explicitly when needed; compare affected Pods and node placement to spot a shared failure domain.

commands.title: Inspect Pod events and conditions
commands.purpose: Read the Pod's current conditions, container state, probe results and recent events.
commands.environment: Replace POD_NAME and NAMESPACE with the real Pod and namespace.
commands.expectedOutput: Pod details followed by container state and an Events section when events are available.
commands.interpretation: Look for scheduling failures, image pull errors, failed probes, mount errors and repeated restarts. Events expire, so absence of an event is not proof that nothing happened.
commands.safety: Read-only command; output may include environment metadata. Avoid sharing sensitive output publicly.

commands.title: Read recent container logs
commands.purpose: Read a bounded tail of the current container logs for a first-pass diagnosis.
commands.environment: Replace the Pod and namespace. Add -c CONTAINER_NAME when the Pod has multiple containers.
commands.expectedOutput: The last 100 log lines available from the selected container.
commands.interpretation: Correlate timestamps with the incident. For a restarted container, consider --previous; logs alone may not explain a scheduling or network issue.
commands.safety: Read-only command; redact tokens, credentials and personal data before sharing logs.

commands.title: Sort recent namespace events
commands.purpose: Review recent events in timestamp order to identify scheduling, image, probe and controller signals.
commands.environment: Replace NAMESPACE; use cluster-wide access only when you have a reason and permission.
commands.expectedOutput: An event list with type, reason, object, message and last timestamp.
commands.interpretation: Prioritize Warning events and correlate them with the affected resource and time window. Event retention is limited.

commands.title: Check Deployment rollout progress
commands.purpose: Wait for and report whether a Deployment rollout has completed.
commands.environment: Replace the Deployment name and namespace.
commands.expectedOutput: A success message when rollout completes, or a waiting/timeout message if it is stalled.
commands.interpretation: If it stalls, inspect the Deployment, ReplicaSets, Pods and events. This command observes progress; it does not itself repair the rollout.
commands.safety: Observational command. It waits until completion unless a timeout is supplied.

commands.title: Inspect current Pod resource usage
commands.purpose: View current CPU and memory usage when Metrics Server or a compatible metrics API is available.
commands.environment: Requires the metrics API to be installed and reporting data.
commands.expectedOutput: A table of Pod names and current CPU/memory usage.
commands.interpretation: Compare usage with requests and limits; this is a point-in-time sample, not a historical graph or root-cause explanation.

debugging.title: Pod remains Pending
debugging.symptom: A Pod has stayed Pending longer than expected.

steps.action: Inspect Pod scheduling conditions and events.
steps.evidence: Look for insufficient CPU/memory, unbound PVCs, taints, affinity constraints or missing tolerations.

steps.action: Check node capacity and allocatable resources.
steps.evidence: Compare requested resources and node conditions; do not infer capacity from current CPU utilisation alone.

steps.action: Check storage claims if events mention volumes.
steps.evidence: A Pending claim can block Pod scheduling when the workload requires that volume.

debugging.avoid: Do not delete and recreate the Pod repeatedly before understanding the scheduling constraint.

debugging.title: Container repeatedly restarts
debugging.symptom: A container enters CrashLoopBackOff or its restart count rises quickly.

steps.action: Inspect last termination reason and recent events.
steps.evidence: Check exit code, OOMKilled state, failed probes, mount errors and restart backoff.

steps.action: Read current and previous container logs.
steps.command: kubectl logs POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE --tail=100; kubectl logs POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE --previous
steps.evidence: Compare startup errors with the prior container attempt; redact secrets before sharing output.

steps.action: Compare the latest rollout and configuration changes.
steps.evidence: A failure aligned with a rollout may point to a bad image, configuration or dependency.

debugging.avoid: Do not blindly increase liveness thresholds or roll back without checking the blast radius and current rollout state.

debugging.title: Service has no ready endpoints
debugging.symptom: A Service exists but requests fail or no ready backend endpoints appear.

steps.evidence: Verify the selector matches intended Pod labels.
No ready endpoints can indicate selector mismatch or Pods failing readiness.

steps.action: Verify port mapping and network policy only after confirming backends.
steps.evidence: Confirm targetPort matches the container's listening port and examine applicable policy if routing still fails.

debugging.avoid: Do not expose a workload publicly as a shortcut for an internal Service connectivity problem.
